description:
Lunar Flames 🔥🌙

We are a team of passionate innovators exploring the intersection of space science, artificial intelligence, and technology. Driven by curiosity and creativity, we aim to turn complex scientific challenges into meaningful solutions.

For NASA Space Apps Challenge, we are focused on exploring fire behavior in microgravity and leveraging AI and data-driven insights to support better understanding of fire safety beyond Earth.

Igniting Innovation Beyond Gravity.🔥🚀
summary:
Flame in Freefall is a local research dashboard prototype that organises NASA microgravity combustion research. We built it with Python, FastAPI, SQLite, Pandas, PyMuPDF, HTML/CSS/JavaScript and Chart.js. It catalogues 16 NASA investigations. It imports CSV measurements (384 rows from PSI-25 BASS-II so far) and extracts text from uploaded PDFs. A keyword retrieval assistant returns matching source passages. It is not generative AI. Users can compare investigations, view charts and see a transparent, point-based relevance ranking. That ranking is a heuristic, not a fire-risk score.

It addresses the challenge by gathering scattered NASA fire-behaviour research into one searchable, comparable place. It keeps catalogue metadata separate from measurement data, cites sources and never invents missing values.

It matters because flames behave very differently without gravity, so Earth-based fire-safety assumptions cannot simply be carried into spacecraft. Making microgravity combustion research easier to find and compare supports safer space exploration. Future work includes more NASA datasets, better discovery and richer visualisation.
details:
What it does and how it works

Flame in Freefall is a local web dashboard for exploring NASA microgravity combustion research. The backend is written in Python with FastAPI and stores data in SQLite. Users can:

  • Browse and search a catalogue of 16 NASA investigations, such as BASS-II, SAFFIRE, SAME, FLEX and ACME.
  • Import CSV measurement data. We have loaded 384 rows from PSI-25 BASS-II.
  • Upload PDFs, which are split into searchable text chunks.
  • Ask questions. A keyword retrieval assistant returns the matching source passages with links.
  • Compare investigations side by side and view charts.
  • See a relevance ranking based on a published point system.

Benefits

Microgravity fire research is spread across many records, files and papers. The dashboard puts it in one place, so it is faster to find, compare and cite.

Intended impact

We want to make it easier for students, researchers and developers to discover and understand how fire behaves without gravity. That knowledge supports safer spacecraft and habitat design.

Tools and technologies

Python, FastAPI, SQLite, Pandas (CSV handling), PyMuPDF (PDF text extraction), HTML, CSS, JavaScript and Chart.js. It runs locally on an ordinary computer, so no special hardware is needed. We used public NASA PSI data as the source.

Creativity

The interface is built as a mission-control-style research workspace, with an overview, explorer, ranking, assistant and data views. The assistant retrieves evidence and does not generate answers. The ranking logic is visible. Together these make it a transparent alternative to a black-box AI.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific integrity: missing values stay blank, nothing is estimated, and catalogue descriptions are kept separate from experimental measurements.
  • Honest limits: ranking is a heuristic and not a fire-risk prediction, and the assistant is retrieval-only.
  • Data boundaries: only BASS-II has measurements loaded, and no partial-gravity data is included.
  • Source citation: every NASA source should be cited with its identifier and URL.
  • Practicality: free tools and local-first operation, so anyone can run it.

Future work

More NASA datasets, better discovery, wider analytics and richer visualisation.
